title: What do instructional designers charge per hour: a guide for freelance Mac users

intro: Instructional designers typically charge between $50 and $150 per hour depending on experience, complexity, and industry. Many freelancers find that answering what do instructional designers charge per hour is difficult because there is no single industry standard or fixed salary model.
tldr: Most freelancers start with an hourly rate but move to project-based pricing to reward efficiency.
Calculate your rate by adding business costs and taxes to your desired income then dividing by billable hours.
Avoid the underpricing spiral by accounting for non-billable time like marketing and admin.

stats.label: Burnout rate among freelancers with 0 to 1 years of experience

blocks.text: Why setting freelance rates is hard

When you work for a company, your salary is set. As a freelancer, you become a business owner. You must account for taxes, software subscriptions, insurance, and professional development. Many instructional designers struggle to set rates because they do not account for non-billable time. You might work eight hours, but only four are billable. If you only charge for those four hours without accounting for the other four, you lose money.

Many new freelancers undercharge to land contracts quickly. This creates an underpricing spiral. You must work more hours to meet your income goals. This leads to exhaustion and burnout. You cannot provide high-quality design work when you are burnt out. The goal is to set a rate that covers your life and your business growth.
How to calculate your hourly rate

Calculate your rate backwards. Start with your target annual income. Add your business expenses, including taxes. A common estimate for taxes is 30 percent. Divide this total by your actual billable hours. Many freelancers estimate that only 60 percent of their total work time is billable. Do not guess your rate. Use the math to find the floor for your pricing.

A common industry rule is to double your previous full-time hourly rate. If you earned $35 per hour as an employee, a sustainable freelance rate is often near $70 per hour. This covers the overhead that your previous employer paid for you. Remember that these numbers are benchmarks. Your specific industry, such as higher education or corporate training, will change these figures.

Hourly rates can punish efficiency. If you become faster, you earn less. As you gain experience, move to value-based pricing. Price projects based on the value you deliver to the client. Consider the time a typical specialist would spend on the task. Do not price based solely on your own speed.

Always use a contract. Define your scope clearly. List payment terms and fees for extra rounds of review. This prevents profit erosion from scope creep. If a client asks for more work, refer back to the contract. It is the best tool you have to protect your time and your income.

faq.question: Should I charge hourly or by the project?
faq.answer: Hourly is safer for beginners. Project-based pricing is better for experienced designers who have a clear understanding of their own speed and project requirements.

faq.question: How do I deal with clients who think my rate is too high?
faq.answer: Focus on the value you provide. Explain the outcomes of your work. If they still cannot meet your rate, they may not be the right client for your business.

faq.question: What if I am just starting out?
faq.answer: Start with a rate that covers your living and business expenses. Use the backward calculation method to ensure you are not losing money.

causes.title: No standardized pricing
causes.text: The industry lacks a universal rate, making it hard to know where to start.

causes.title: Ignoring non-billable time
causes.text: Designers fail to account for the time spent on marketing, admin, and proposals.

causes.title: Underpricing to compete
causes.text: New freelancers often lower rates to win their first few projects.

fixes.title: Calculate backwards
fixes.text: Determine your target income, add 30 percent for taxes and expenses, and divide by billable hours.

fixes.title: Use contracts
fixes.text: Clearly define project scope and extra fees to prevent scope creep.

fixes.title: Shift to value-based pricing
fixes.text: Price based on the value of the outcome rather than just the hours you spend.
